gloss: put, set, place; appoint; make (into); ordain
summary: The verb is to put a thing in its place: the man in the garden, a stone under the head, the tablets in the ark, words in a mouth. From that it is to set up or station (a pillar, an ambush), to lay a thing on someone (a burden, a charge, a name), to set a man over others, to make a thing into something else (a wilderness into a pool, Abraham's seed as the dust), and to fix what is to stand: a statute, a covenant, the bound of the sea. With heart, face or eye it is to turn one's attention or purpose on something. Yahweh is its commonest subject in the prophets and the psalms; it stands beside נָתַן, which shares “put, set, make” but starts from giving. The Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra uses שִׂים the same way, above all in שִׂים טְעֵם “issue a decree”, and the Peshitta's ܣܡ (sām) is its verb for laying a body in a tomb, laying hands on the sick, appointing, and laying down one's soul.

words.gloss: put, set, place; set up; lay on; appoint; make (into); ordain; turn (heart, face, eye) to
words.summary: About 585 times, nearly all in the qal. The dictionary form is written שִׂים or שׂוּם: the imperfect is יָשִׂים (once יָשׂוּם, Exo 4:11), the imperative שִׂים, the infinitive שׂוּם or שִׂים, the infinitive absolute שׂוֹם. Its core is putting a thing where it is to be; the other uses are that act with a person, an office, a result or a rule in view, and the preposition shows which (בְּ “in”, עַל “on, over”, לְ “for, as, into”, לִפְנֵי “before”). The token count includes the Aramaic forms spelled alike and the one passive participle שׂוּמָה (2Sa 13:32), which is filed apart as a noun but is a form of this verb.

stems.gloss: put, set, place; set up, station; lay on, impose; appoint; make (into); ordain, establish; give a name; turn (heart, face, eye) to; grant

senses.definition: To put a thing or a person in or on a place, so that it is there: in a garden, in an ark, in a basket, under the head, on the shoulder, on the neck, in the hand.

evidence.note: “Yahweh God planted a garden in Eden … וַיָּשֶׂם שָׁם the man whom he had formed”: the first use, a person put in a place.
“וָאָשִׂם the tablets in the ark which I had made, and they were there”: what is put stays where it is put.
Jacob took one of the stones of the place “and put it at his head”.
Moses' mother put the child in the ark, and put the ark in the reeds.
The first of the fruit: “you shall put it in a basket”.
Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering “and laid it on Isaac his son”.
“Put your hand under my thigh”: so also Gen 47:29.
Pharaoh “put the chain of gold on his neck”.
Jacob “put sackcloth on his loins”.
“Put your garments on you.”
“You shall put (וְנָתַתָּ) oil on it and lay (וְשַׂמְתָּ) frankincense on it”: beside נָתַן in the same sense.
“Lay my staff on the face of the boy.”
Jael “took the hammer in her hand” (put it in her hand).
“My hand I lay on my mouth.”
“I will put you in a cleft of the rock.”
The infinitive as a noun: “from the placing of man on earth” (מִנִּי שִׂים אָדָם עֲלֵי אָרֶץ).

senses.definition: To set a thing up to stand, or to post men in a position: a pillar, an altar, an image, an ambush, a garrison, a siege, companies of fighting men.

evidence.note: The stone which he had put (שָׂם) at his head “he set up (וַיָּשֶׂם) as a pillar”: both senses in one verse.
“Set yourself an ambush for the city behind it.”
Saul “set the people in three companies”; so the Chaldeans in Job 1:17.
David “set garrisons in Aram of Damascus”.
Ben-hadad to his servants: “שִׂימוּ”, and “they set themselves against the city”: the verb alone, of drawing up for the attack.
“Set battering rams against it all around.”
Jehu “had set for himself eighty men outside”.
“You have set up altars to the shameful thing.”
Manasseh “set the carved image of the Asherah in the house” where Yahweh had said he would set his name.
“Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole … and Moses made a serpent of bronze and set it on the pole.”

senses.definition: With עַל or בְּ of the person: to lay on someone a burden, a task, a tribute, a disease, interest, or guilt; to charge someone with a thing.

evidence.note: Moses: “why have I not found favour in your eyes, לָשׂוּם the burden of all this people on me?”
“The tally of bricks which they made before you shall lay on them; you shall not lessen it.”
“You shall not lay interest on him.”
Hezekiah: “what you put (תִּתֵּן) on me I will bear”; and the king of Assyria “laid on (וַיָּשֶׂם עַל) Hezekiah three hundred talents of silver”: נָתַן and שִׂים for the one act.
“All the sickness which I laid on Egypt I will not lay on you.”
That the blood of the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might be laid on Abimelech their brother.
The parapet for the roof: “you shall not put blood on your house”, that is, bloodguilt.
“He lays against her wanton charges.”
Ahimelech: “let not the king lay a thing against (יָשֵׂם בְּ) his servant”: to impute.
“His messengers he charges with error.”

senses.gloss: appoint, set over, make (ruler, judge, king)
senses.definition: With עַל “over”, or a second noun, or לְ: to set a man in an office over others, as prince, judge, head, lord or king.

evidence.note: “Who made you (מִי שָׂמְךָ) a prince and a judge over us?” Stephen quotes it twice (Act 7:27, 35).
Exo 2:14 quoted: “Who appointed you (τίς σε κατέστησεν) ruler and judge over us?”
“This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who appointed you ruler and judge?, him God sent as ruler and redeemer.”
“You shall surely set over you (שׂוֹם תָּשִׂים עָלֶיךָ) a king whom Yahweh your God chooses … you may not put (לָתֵת) over you a foreigner”: again beside נָתַן.
The elders to Samuel: “set us a king to judge us, like all the nations”.
Joseph: “God has made me (וַיְשִׂימֵנִי) a father to Pharaoh and lord of all his house … God has made me lord of all Egypt”.
Of Joseph: “he made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession”; Stephen's “he appointed him governor over Egypt and all his house” (Act 7:10).
“Set over them princes of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens.”
“I will set them as your heads.”
Samuel “made his sons judges for Israel”.
The people “set him over them as head and chief”.
“They set over him princes of forced labour.”
The sons of Judah and the sons of Israel gathered together “shall set for themselves one head”.

senses.definition: With a second noun, or לְ, or כְּ: to make a person or thing into something else, or like something else. Yahweh is nearly always the subject: he makes a nation of one man, a pool of a wilderness, a waste of a city.

evidence.note: Of Ishmael: “the son of the slave woman also I will make into a nation (לְגוֹי אֲשִׂימֶנּוּ)”; so 21:18 and, of Jacob in Egypt, 46:3.
“I will make your seed as the dust of the earth”; “as the sand of the sea” in Gen 32:13.
“I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water”; the same words in Psa 107:35, and the reverse in Psa 107:33.
Yahweh “made the sea dry land”.
“Woe to those who put darkness for light and light for darkness, bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter.”
“I will make darkness light before them.”
“I will make Samaria a heap of the field.”
“Esau I hated, and I made his mountains a desolation.”
“Who made (מִי שָׂם) a mouth for man? or who makes (יָשׂוּם) dumb or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?”
Isaac to Esau: “a master I have made him (שַׂמְתִּיו) over you, and all his brothers I have given (נָתַתִּי) him as servants”.
Of the servant: “when his soul makes (תָּשִׂים) a guilt offering” (or “when you make his soul a guilt offering”), “he shall see seed, he shall prolong days”.
Zion, forsaken and hated: “I will make you an everlasting pride”.
“I will make them a praise and a name in all the earth.”
“You make me head of nations.”
To Zerubbabel: “I will make you like a signet, for I have chosen you”.

senses.gloss: ordain, establish, fix (a statute, a covenant, a bound, a time, a sign)
senses.definition: To set a thing so that it stands and binds: a statute and judgment, a law, a covenant, the bound of the sea and the measures of the earth, an appointed time, a place, a sign.

evidence.note: At Marah: “there he set for him (שָׂם לוֹ) a statute and a judgment”; the same words of Joshua at Shechem (Jos 24:25).
“He raised up (וַיָּקֶם) a testimony in Jacob, and a law he set (שָׂם) in Israel”: parallel to הֵקִים.
Joseph “made it a statute (וַיָּשֶׂם אֹתָהּ לְחֹק) to this day”; so David in 1Sa 30:25.
“These are the judgments which you shall set before them”; Deu 4:44, “this is the law which Moses set before the sons of Israel”.
David: “an everlasting covenant he has made (שָׂם) for me, ordered in all and kept”.
“If I have not established (שָׂמְתִּי) my covenant of day and night, the statutes of heavens and earth.”
“I set the sand as a bound for the sea, an everlasting statute, and it does not pass over it.”
“A bound you set which they shall not pass; they shall not return to cover the earth.”
“When he set (בְּשׂוּמוֹ) for the sea its statute.”
“Who set its measures?”; 38:33, “do you set its rule on the earth?”
“Yahweh set an appointed time (מוֹעֵד), saying, Tomorrow.”
“I will appoint you a place to which he shall flee.”
“I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and plant them.”
“Yahweh set a sign for Cain.”
“He set his signs in Egypt”; so Exo 10:2, Jer 32:20, Isa 66:19.
Of the servant: “he shall not grow dim or be crushed until he sets judgment in the earth”; Matthew gives it “until he brings forth judgment to victory” (Mat 12:20).

senses.gloss: give a name; set (one's) name on or in
senses.definition: With שֵׁם: to give someone a name; to make a name for oneself; and, of Yahweh, to set his name in the place he chooses and on his people.

evidence.note: “The chief of the eunuchs gave them names (וַיָּשֶׂם לָהֶם שֵׁמוֹת): he gave to Daniel Belteshazzar.”
“You chose Abram … and made his name Abraham (וְשַׂמְתָּ שְּׁמוֹ אַבְרָהָם).”
Gideon's concubine bore a son “and he set his name Abimelech”.
“The sons of Jacob, whose name he made Israel.”
God went to redeem a people for himself “and to make himself a name”.
“The place which Yahweh your God shall choose out of all your tribes to set his name there (לָשׂוּם אֶת שְׁמוֹ שָׁם), for his dwelling.”
“I have made holy this house which you have built, to set my name there for ever.”
“In this house and in Jerusalem … I will set my name for ever.”
After the priests' blessing: “they shall set my name on the sons of Israel, and I will bless them.”

senses.gloss: set (heart, face, eye) on: consider; purpose; regard
senses.definition: With לֵב “heart”: to give one's mind to a thing, consider it, take it to heart; with פָּנִים “face”: to turn toward, to purpose to go, or to turn against; with עַיִן “eye”: to look on, for good or for evil.

evidence.note: “He who did not set his heart to the word of Yahweh left his servants and his cattle in the field”: against “he who feared the word of Yahweh” in the verse before.
“Set your heart on your ways”: consider them.
Yahweh to the adversary: “have you set your heart on my servant Job?”
“The righteous perishes, and no man lays it to heart.”
“Set your heart to all the words which I testify among you today.”
“David laid these words in his heart, and feared greatly.”
“Daniel set on his heart that he would not defile himself”: resolved.
The verb alone: “that they may see and know and consider (וְיָשִׂימוּ) and understand together”.
Jacob “set his face toward the hill country of Gilead”: the direction he meant to go.
“Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem.”
The servant: “I have set my face like flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed.”
Jesus “set his face firmly to go to Jerusalem”: the Hebrew phrase.
“Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy to them.”
“I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good”; so Lev 20:5 of the man who gives his seed to Molech.
Joseph: “bring him down to me, that I may set my eye on him.”
“I will set my eye on them for good”; “for evil and not for good” in Amo 9:4.

senses.definition: To give someone the words he is to speak: Yahweh to a prophet, Moses to Aaron, Joab to the woman of Tekoa.

evidence.note: “You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth.”
Balaam: “the word which God puts in my mouth, that I shall speak”; and Yahweh did so (23:5).
“I have put my words in your mouth.”
“My spirit which is on you and my words which I have put in your mouth shall not depart from your mouth.”
The song of Moses: “teach it to the sons of Israel; put it in their mouths”.
“Joab put the words in her mouth.”

senses.gloss: grant, give (peace, mercy, glory, a remnant)
senses.definition: With לְ of the person: to grant or give him a thing. Here the verb meets נָתַן, and the two stand side by side.

evidence.note: “Yahweh lift up his face to you and give you (וְיָשֵׂם לְךָ) peace.”
“My son, give (שִׂים) glory to Yahweh God of Israel, and give (וְתֶן) him praise”: שִׂים and נָתַן in parallel.
“To appoint (לָשׂוּם) for the mourners of Zion, to give (לָתֵת) them a headdress instead of ashes.”
“Let them give glory to Yahweh.”
Babylon: “you showed them no mercy” (לֹא שַׂמְתְּ לָהֶם רַחֲמִים).
“God sent me before you to set for you a remnant in the earth.”

senses.definition: The qal's passive forms: וַיִּישֶׂם “he was put”, and the passive participle שׂוּמָה, “a thing set”, of a purpose fixed.

evidence.note: Joseph died, they embalmed him, “וַיִּישֶׂם in a coffin in Egypt”: he was put.
Jonadab of Amnon's death: “by the mouth of Absalom it has been settled (הָיְתָה שׂוּמָה) from the day he humbled Tamar his sister”.

senses.definition: Twice only, both in poetry and both without an object: of the sword told to set itself to the right or the left, and of men who perish with none giving heed. Each is the qal's “set” with its object (face, heart) left unsaid.

evidence.note: To the sword: “go right, הָשִׂימִי, go left, wherever your face is appointed”.
“From morning to evening they are crushed; with none heeding (מִבְּלִי מֵשִׂים) they perish for ever”: as אֵין אִישׁ שָׂם עַל לֵב in Isa 57:1.

senses.definition: Once, as the text is read (וַיּוּשַׂם; written ויישם, the form of Gen 50:26): food was set before Abraham's servant.

evidence.note: “And there was set before him to eat; and he said, I will not eat until I have spoken my words.”

evidence.locator: Gen.2.8, וַיָּשֶׂם → ἔθετο; Exo.15.25, שָׂם → ἔθετο; 1Sa.19.5, וַיָּשֶׂם → ἔθετο; 1Sa.21.13, וַיָּשֶׂם → ἔθετο; Job.13.14, אָשִׂים → θήσω; Isa.42.4, יָשִׂים → θῇ; τίθημι renders שִׂים ×221

evidence.note: “The good shepherd lays down his soul (τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τίθησιν) for the sheep”: the Hebrew שִׂים נֶפֶשׁ, as in “he put his soul in his palm” (1Sa 19:5). The Peshitta has ܣܐܡ (sāʾem), this root.
“Settle it in your hearts (θέσθε εἰς τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν)”: the Hebrew שִׂים בַּלֵּב of 1Sa 21:13; so Luk 1:66 and Act 5:4.

evidence.locator: Exo.2.14, שָׂמְךָ → κατέστησεν; Psa.105.21, שָׂמוֹ → κατέστησεν; Deu.17.15, שׂוֹם תָּשִׂים → καθιστῶν καταστήσεις; καθίστημι renders שִׂים ×11 and more

evidence.note: Exo 2:14 quoted: “τίς σε κατέστησεν ἄρχοντα καὶ δικαστὴν ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς;”
Of Joseph, as Psa 105:21: “he appointed him governor over Egypt and all his house”.

evidence.locator: Ezk.6.2, שִׂים פָּנֶיךָ → στήρισον; Ezk.21.2, שִׂים → στήρισον; Jer.21.10, שַׂמְתִּי פָנַי → ἐστήρικα; στηρίζω renders שִׂים ×10

evidence.note: “He set his face firmly (τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἐστήριξεν) to go to Jerusalem”: the prophets' שִׂים פָּנִים in its Septuagint dress.

parallels.note: “Give; put, set, make”. The two verbs share put, set, appoint, make and grant, and scripture often uses them together for variety. They differ in where they start: נָתַן is handing over, so it alone is used of giving land, a wife, wages or a city into a hand; שִׂים is placing, so it is the usual verb for fixing a statute or a bound, for setting heart, face and eye, and for turning one thing into another.

evidence.note: “אֶתֵּן in the wilderness the cedar … אָשִׂים in the desert the cypress.”
Oil put (נָתַן), frankincense laid (שִׂים).
“You shall set (תָּשִׂים) a king over you … you may not put (לָתֵת) a foreigner over you.”
“A master I have made him (שַׂמְתִּיו) … his brothers I have given (נָתַתִּי) him as servants.”
“Give (שִׂים) glory … give (תֶן) praise.”

parallels.note: “Put, set”: the nearest verb in sense, in parallel with שִׂים in the prophets.

evidence.note: “וְשַׂמְתִּיהָ like the wilderness, וְשַׁתִּהָ like a dry land.”
“You look for light, and he makes it (וְשָׂמָהּ) the shadow of death, and turns it (written ישית) to thick darkness.”

parallels.note: “Raise up, establish”: of a testimony and a law.
“Found”: of what Yahweh has appointed and founded.

evidence.note: “Yahweh, for judgment you have appointed him (שַׂמְתּוֹ); Rock, for reproof you have founded him (יְסַדְתּוֹ).”
“Give him no rest until he establishes (יְכוֹנֵן) and until he makes (יָשִׂים) Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

opposites.note: “Take away, remove”: what is taken off against what is put on.

evidence.note: “Take away (הָסִירוּ) the filthy garments from him … let them set (יָשִׂימוּ) a clean turban on his head.”

phrases.gloss: set the heart (on, to): consider, pay heed; also שִׂים עַל לֵב, lay to heart

evidence.note: “If you will not lay it to heart to give glory to my name.”

phrases.gloss: set the face: turn toward, purpose to go; with בְּ, set the face against

evidence.note: “If you indeed set your faces to go to Egypt.”

phrases.gloss: set the eye on: look on, look after

evidence.note: Nebuchadnezzar of Jeremiah: “take him and set your eyes on him, and do him no harm.”

phrases.gloss: put one's soul in one's palm: risk one's life

evidence.note: Of David: “he put his soul in his palm and struck the Philistine.”

phrases.gloss: put a word in the mouth of: tell what to say
give a name; (of Yahweh) set his name there
set a statute and a judgment

evidence.note: “On the right path is the man who has made Yahweh his trust.”
“That they should set their hope in God.”
“If I have made gold my hope.”
“Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm.”

phrases.gloss: giving the sense (of what is read)

evidence.note: “They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly, וְשׂוֹם שֶׂכֶל, and they understood the reading.”

words.gloss: set, put; issue (a decree); appoint; pay (regard)
words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra, about 26 times: the token count is far higher only because Hebrew forms spelled alike (שָׂם, שִׂים, שָׂמוּ) are counted with it. Most uses are the chancery phrase שִׂים טְעֵם, “set a decree”, of a king's order; the rest show the Hebrew verb's senses: appoint, give a name, set the mind, lay a stone.

stems.gloss: issue (a decree); appoint; give (a name); pay (regard); set (the mind)

senses.definition: With טְעֵם: of a king, to give an order that binds.

evidence.note: “In the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king שָׂם טְעֵם to build this house of God.”
“You, O king, have made a decree (שָׂמְתָּ טְּעֵם) that every man who hears the sound of the horn … shall fall down.”
“Who gave you a decree to build this house?”
“I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with diligence.”

senses.gloss: pay regard to; set the mind on
senses.definition: With טְעֵם and עַל of a person: to pay him regard; with בָּל “mind”: to set one's mind on doing a thing.

evidence.note: “These men have not paid regard to you (לָא שָׂמוּ עֲלָךְ טְעֵם), O king: your gods they do not serve.”
“Daniel … has paid no regard to you, O king, nor to the interdict.”
The king “set his mind on Daniel (עַל דָּנִיֵּאל שָׂם בָּל) to deliver him”.

senses.definition: To set a man in an office.

evidence.note: The vessels were given “to one named Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor (דִּי פֶחָה שָׂמֵהּ)”.

senses.definition: With שֻׁם: to give someone a name.

evidence.note: “Daniel, whose name the king made Belteshazzar (שָׂם שְׁמֵהּ בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר)”: the Aramaic of the Hebrew in Dan 1:7.

senses.definition: The passive of the peal: of a decree, מִנִּי שִׂים טְעֵם, “from me a decree is made”; and of a stone laid on the mouth of the den.

evidence.note: “From me a decree is made (וּמִנִּי שִׂים טְעֵם) that every people, nation and tongue …”
“A stone was brought and laid (וְשֻׂמַת) on the mouth of the den.”

stems.gloss: be set; be made (into); be issued

senses.gloss: be laid (timber); be made (a dunghill); be issued (a decree)
senses.definition: Passive in the three chief senses of the verb: put in place, made into, decreed.

evidence.note: The house is being built of great stones, “and timber is being set (מִתְּשָׂם) in the walls”.
“Your houses shall be made (יִתְּשָׂמוּן) a dunghill.”
“Until the decree is issued (יִתְּשָׂם) by me.”
Joseph “laid it (ἔθηκεν) in his own new tomb … and rolled a great stone to the door”: the same verb of the same act as the stone laid on the den.

phrases.gloss: issue a decree; with עַל of a person, pay regard to

words.gloss: put, lay, place; appoint; lay down (the soul)
words.summary: The Peshitta's ܣܡ (sām), about 200 times, with s for the Hebrew ś as Syriac always writes it. It is the usual verb where the Greek has τίθημι and ἐπιτίθημι: laying a body in a tomb, laying hands on someone, setting a thing before people, appointing, and laying down one's soul.

stems.gloss: put, lay; lay (hands) on; appoint, make; lay down (the soul); set (in the heart, the mind)

senses.definition: To put a thing or a body in a place.

evidence.note: Joseph “laid it (וסָמֵה) in his new tomb”.
“They have taken our Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him.”
They “laid it at the feet of the apostles”.
“Another foundation than this which is laid (דּסִימָא) no man can lay (לַמסָם), which is Jesus Christ.”
Isa 42:1, where the Hebrew has נָתַתִּי: “my spirit I will put (אֵסִים) on him”.

senses.definition: With ܐܝܕܐ “hand”: to lay the hand on someone, to heal or to bless.

evidence.note: “My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand on her (סִים אִידָך עלֵיה), and she will live.”
He took the children in his arms “and laid his hand on them and blessed them”.

senses.definition: To set someone in a place or office, or make him something.

evidence.note: Gen 17:5 quoted: “a father to a multitude of peoples I have made you (דּסָמתָּך)”, where the Hebrew has נְתַתִּיךָ.
Isa 49:6 quoted: “I have set you a light to the peoples.”
His son, “whom he appointed (סָם) heir of all things”.
“I chose you and appointed you (וסָמתּכֻון) that you should go and bear fruit.”
“God has set in his ecclesia first apostles, after them prophets.”
Psa 110:1 quoted: “until I put your enemies under your feet”.

senses.definition: With ܢܦܫܐ “soul”: to give up one's life for another.

evidence.note: “The good shepherd lays down his soul (נַפשֵה סָאֵם) for his flock.”
“I lay down my soul that I may take it again … I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it again; this command I received from my Father.”
“Greater love than this there is not, that a man lay down his soul for his friends.”

senses.gloss: set (in the heart, the mind); set (the face)
senses.definition: To settle a thing in one's heart or mind, to purpose; of the face, set toward a place.

evidence.note: “Set it in your hearts (סִימו בּלֵבּכֻון) not to be learning beforehand to make a defence.”
“Why did you set in your heart to do this thing?”
“Paul set in his mind” to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem.
The Samaritans did not receive him “because his face was set (סִים) to go to Jerusalem”.

stems.gloss: be laid; be laid on; be appointed

senses.gloss: be laid (in a tomb); be laid on (a burden); be appointed
senses.definition: The passive of the peal, in the form ܐܬܬܣܝܡ (ettsīm).

evidence.note: A tomb “in which no one had yet been laid (אֵתּתּסִים)”; so Jhn 19:41.
The women “saw where he was laid”.
Jacob and the fathers were carried to Shechem “and laid in the tomb which Abraham bought”.
“That no greater burden be laid on you than these necessary things.”
“Of which I was appointed herald and apostle.”

words.gloss: treasure (what is laid up); placing, in “placing of sons” (adoption)
words.summary: The Peshitta's ܣܝܡܬܐ (sīmtā), “a thing laid up”: treasure, where the Greek has θησαυρός; and in ܣܝܡܬ ܒܢܝܐ (sīmaṯ bnayyā; in the text סִימַת בּנַיָא), “the placing of sons”, for υἱοθεσία, adoption, which is the same compound in Greek (υἱός “son” with θέσις “placing”).

senses.definition: What has been laid up and kept: wealth, and what a man values above it.

evidence.note: “Where your treasure (סִימַתכֻון) is, there is your heart also.”
“The kingdom of the heavens is like a treasure hidden in the field.”
“We have this treasure in a vessel of earthenware.”
“In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and of knowledge.”

senses.definition: In ܣܝܡܬ ܒܢܝܐ: being set in the place of sons.

evidence.note: “You have received the spirit of the placing of sons (דּסִימַת בּנַיָא), by which we cry, Abba, our Father.”
“That we might receive the placing of sons.”
The sons of Israel, “whose was the placing of sons, and the glory, and the covenants”.

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܣܝܡܐ (syāmā), “a placing”, only in ܣܝܡ ܐܝܕܐ (syām īḏā), “the laying on of the hand”, for ἐπίθεσις τῶν χειρῶν. It is the noun of the verb's “lay the hand on”; no cognate noun is cited for it, and its tie to the root rests on that verb.

senses.definition: The act of laying the hand on a person, by which the apostles gave the holy spirit and a gift was given to Timothy.

evidence.note: “Simon saw that by the laying on of the hand of the apostles (בַסיָם אִידָא) the holy spirit was given.”
“The gift that is in you, which was given you by prophecy and by the laying on of the hand of the eldership.”
“The gift of God which is in you by the laying on of my hand.”
Among the first things: “the teaching of baptism and of the laying on of the hand”.

words.gloss: a thing put (in the hand): deposit, pledge
words.summary: Once only, in תְּשׂוּמֶת יָד, “a putting of the hand”, so its meaning rests on that one verse: something put into a man's hand by his neighbour, named beside the פִּקָּדוֹן, the thing left in his keeping. Whether it is a deposit, a pledge or a loan the verse does not say. It is formed from the verb as תְּרוּמָה is from רוּם; no cognate noun is cited for it.

senses.gloss: what is put in the hand (deposit or pledge)
senses.definition: A thing entrusted by one man to another, about which the holder might lie to his neighbour.

evidence.note: “If a soul sins … and lies to his fellow about a thing left in his keeping (בְּפִקָּדוֹן) or בִתְשׂוּמֶת יָד or a robbery, or has oppressed his fellow.”

cognates.gloss: put, place; establish, make; erect (a stele)
cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic use the verb as Hebrew does: of things put in a coffin (the Eshmunazar inscription, “they did not put anything in it”), of an agreement made, and of a stele set up to a god, as Jacob set up his stone (Gen 28:18). Phoenician writes one letter for š and ś.

evidence.note: “[Heb. ś-m] v. qal 1. PUT, PLACE, KAI 14.4/5 … 2. ESTABLISH, MAKE … 3. ERECT a stele, KAI 61 A 1/5” (read from the PDF's text layer).

cognates.gloss: set up, prepare, establish; appoint (to an office); (noun) patron deity (Sabaean)
cognates.note: Sabaean keeps the old ś as its own letter (s²), as Hebrew does with שׂ. The verb's first two senses are the Hebrew's: “he set up an altar”, “(the god) appointed for Y. one as overseer”; the noun s²ym, a tribe's patron deity, is taken as its participle, “the one who appoints”.

evidence.locator: pp. 515–516, ŚYM I (verb) and ŚYM n.
evidence.note: “(1) SET UP, PREPARE, ESTABLISH … C382/1 ‘he set up an altar’ … (2) APPOINT s.o. to an office … PATRON DEITY … [Phps act. prt of v ŚYM in sense ‘appoint’]” (OCR read; the sibilant is lost in the OCR text and is restored from the entry's place in the alphabet and its Hebrew comparison).

cognates.note: Akkadian has the root only in the sense “fix, decree”: of gods and kings determining what shall be. That is the Hebrew verb's “set a statute” (Exo 15:25; Jer 33:25) and the Aramaic שִׂים טְעֵם, “set a decree”. Akkadian š answers to Hebrew שׂ as well as שׁ.

evidence.note: Meanings in the glossaries: fix, decree, determine, destine, be decreed, be determined; 670 instances.

cognates.gloss: what is fixed: destiny, fate; will, testament
cognates.note: The noun of šiāmu, “the thing fixed”: a lot decreed, and a man's last will.

evidence.locator: armep x000129980, šīmtu [what is fixed] N
evidence.note: Meanings: what is fixed, destiny, fate, death, will.

cognates.gloss: insert (a thing in a thing); sheathe (a sword); hide
cognates.note: Arabic ش answers regularly to Hebrew שׂ. The Arabic verb has kept only the narrow sense of putting one thing into another, a sword into its sheath, arrows into the quiver; it shares the Hebrew's “put in”, not its “appoint” or “make”.

evidence.note: “He hid, or concealed, the thing in the thing … and he inserted the thing in the thing. [Hence,] شام سَيْفَهُ … He sheathed his sword … شام نَبْلَهُ [He put his arrows into the quiver].”

cognates.note: The Targums' verb, written with ס or with שׂ, as at Onkelos Lev 19:14 for the Hebrew “you shall not put a stumbling block”.

evidence.note: “Targ. O. Lev. XIX, 14 תְסִים ed. Berl. (oth. ed. תְשֵׂים) … Part. סָאֵים, סָאֵם … V. שׂוּם.”
“Targ. O. Lev. XIX, 14 … Targ. O. Gen. L, 26 … Ithpe. to be placed. Targ. Hag. II, 15.”

cognates.note: The Targums' word for a treasure or a hidden store, the same noun as the Peshitta's.

evidence.note: “treasure. Targ. Gen. XLIII, 23 … Targ. Prov. XXI, 20 (h. text אוֹצָר).”

doctrine.statement: To “put one's soul in one's palm” is to risk one's life: Jephthah did it when he crossed over against Ammon, and David when he struck the Philistine (Jdg 12:3; 1Sa 19:5). The soul there is the life a man can lose. Isaiah says of Yahweh's servant that his soul is made a guilt offering, and that “he poured out his soul to death” (Isa 53:10, 12). Jesus uses the same phrase of himself: “the good shepherd lays down his soul for the sheep”; “I lay down my soul that I may take it again … this command I received from my Father” (Jhn 10:11, 17–18). From the verses: the soul is not a part of a man that lives on when he dies. It is his life, which Jesus gave up in death as an offering for sin, and which he received again when his Father raised him.

Elihu says of God: “if he set his heart on it, and gathered to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would expire together, and man would return to dust” (Job 34:14–15). The spirit and the breath by which all flesh lives are God's own, lent to it; the psalm says the same of the beasts, “you gather their spirit, they expire, and to their dust they return” (Psa 104:29), and the Preacher of man, “the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7). From the verses: man lives only while God keeps his breath in him, as at the first, when God breathed into his nostrils and he became a living soul (Gen 2:7). When it is withdrawn the man is dust again.

Yahweh God formed the man and “put him” in the garden he had planted (Gen 2:8); Zophar dates all human history “from the placing of man on earth” (Job 20:4). Yahweh asks Job who set the earth's measures (Job 38:5); wisdom was there “when he set for the sea its statute” (Pro 8:29); he set the sand as its bound, “an everlasting statute” (Jer 5:22). The psalm says the deep covered the earth like a garment and the waters stood above the mountains, and then, “a bound you set which they shall not pass; they shall not return to cover the earth” (Psa 104:6, 9), as God promised Noah that there should not again be a flood to destroy the earth (Gen 9:11). He says his covenant of day and night, “the statutes of heavens and earth”, is as sure as his covenant with David (Jer 33:25). And of man's body: “who made a mouth for man, or who makes dumb or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?” (Exo 4:11). From the verses: the earth, the sea and man are where and what they are because God put them so and fixed their limits by decree; man was placed on the earth by God's act, at a beginning from which his history is counted.

Moses told Israel to seek “the place which Yahweh your God shall choose out of all your tribes to set his name there, for his dwelling” (Deu 12:5). When Solomon had built the house, Yahweh said, “I have made holy this house which you have built, to set my name there for ever, and my eyes and my heart shall be there all the days” (1Ki 9:3), and of the city, “in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will set my name for ever” (2Ki 21:7). The name is also set on a people: “they shall set my name on the sons of Israel, and I will bless them” (Num 6:27). Jeremiah says of the time to come, “they shall call Jerusalem the throne of Yahweh, and all the nations shall be gathered to it, to the name of Yahweh, to Jerusalem” (Jer 3:17). From the verses: Yahweh has bound his name to one city on earth, and for ever; its present state does not undo the choice, and the nations are yet to come there to his name.

The law said, “you shall surely set over you a king whom Yahweh your God chooses” (Deu 17:15). When Israel asked Samuel, “set us a king to judge us, like all the nations”, Yahweh said they had rejected him from reigning over them (1Sa 8:5, 7). To David he said, “I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and plant them, and they shall dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more” (2Sa 7:10), and of David's seed, “I will set his seed for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven” (Psa 89:30). The prophets look to that king: Judah and Israel gathered together “shall set for themselves one head” (Hos 2:2); “I will make the lame a remnant, and her that was cast off a strong nation, and Yahweh shall reign over them in mount Zion from now and for ever” (Mic 4:7); the servant “shall not grow dim or be crushed until he sets judgment in the earth” (Isa 42:4); and Yahweh is to be given no rest “until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth” (Isa 62:7). The angel said of Jesus that God would give him the throne of David his father, and that he would reign over the house of Jacob for ever (Luk 1:32–33). From the verses: the king Yahweh chooses is David's seed, Jesus; his throne is David's, in Zion; and what he is to set up is judgment in the earth, over Israel regathered and the nations.

When the people were bitten by serpents, Yahweh told Moses, “make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live”; Moses made a serpent of bronze and set it on the pole, and the bitten man who looked to it lived (Num 21:8–9). Jesus said, “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have life” (Jhn 3:14–15). From the verses: the bronze serpent set up on the pole was a figure of Jesus lifted up on the stake; life came to the dying by looking to what God had set up, and comes now by believing in him.

note: Root: `שׂומ`, the key the database files the words under (the brief's key), kept as it is; no other entry has it. The lemma is given as שִׂים (so natan.json cites it); the infinitive is also שׂוּם. BDB keys: u.ap.aa is the Hebrew verb; u.aq.ab is the supposed noun שׂוּמָה (2Sa 13:32 only), treated here as the verb's qal passive participle; BDB's token list for it is the same 601 tokens as u.ap.aa (filed by spelling), so only u.ap.aa is named, as the README directs, and u.aq.ab is left to no entry; xu.ac.aa is the Aramaic verb (its 121 tokens include Hebrew homographs; about 26 are Aramaic); u.ap.ac is תְּשׂוּמֶת; u.ap.ab is the name Jesimiel (names/jesimiel.json). u.bc.ac and w.bq.bc are cross-references with no tokens. Syriac words are given root `סמ`, as the database keys the Peshitta's root (SEDRA root 1263: lexemes 2114 verb, 2115 syāmā, 2116 sīmtā). The qal passive וַיִּישֶׂם (Gen 50:26) is filed as a qal sense because the schema has no qal-passive stem; Gen 24:33 is filed as hophal by its qere. Not all 580 qal uses were read one by one: the senses were built from about 200 verses read in Hebrew, so a rarer use may be missing (for example Job 36:13 יָשִׂימוּ אָף, Job 23:6 יָשִׂם בִּי, Num 24:23 מִשֻּׂמוֹ אֵל, Job 24:25 וְיָשֵׂם לְאַל, left out as obscure). Biella's s²ym was read from OCR, where the sibilant is lost: check the PDF (pp. 515–516) before review. Krahmalkov's page (466) is taken from the running page numbers in the text layer: check against the PDF. Leads not followed: Ge'ez ሤመ śema “put, appoint” (Leslau 1987 / Dillmann 1865: locator not verified, so not cited; Biella's entry and Wiktionary's Hebrew שם both point to it); Old Aramaic שים in the inscriptions; Arabic شِيمَة “natural disposition” beside Akkadian šīmtu (Wiktionary's suggestion, not checked in Lane); Sabaean senses 3 to 6 in Biella (protect, promise, go to war, consult omens), not followed; whether Ugaritic has the root at all (Segert's glossary has only št, “put”); Payne Smith's fuller senses for sām and its nouns. Septuagint ἐπιτίθημι (×41), ποιέω (×29), δίδωμι (×23), τάσσω (×14) and παρατίθημι (×11) also render the verb but no New Testament passage quoting a verse with it was found for them, so they are not listed under `greek`. Mat 12:20 renders Isa 42:4's עַד יָשִׂים בָּאָרֶץ מִשְׁפָּט freely (ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν); it is cited on the sense, not as a Greek rendering.
